content: The core reduction theorem: evaluating any polynomial f at an integral element x is the same as evaluating the remainder of f modulo the minimal polynomial. This is because the quotient term vanishes (minpoly annihilates x).
Uses the division algorithm: f = (f mod minpoly) + minpoly · (f div minpoly). After evaluating at x, the minpoly term vanishes since minpoly(x) = 0.
The annihilator characterization: f annihilates x if and only if the minimal polynomial divides f. This shows the annihilator ideal is principal, generated by the minimal polynomial.
Congruence modulo the minimal polynomial: two polynomials give the same value at x iff they differ by a multiple of the minimal polynomial. This is the polynomial analog of modular arithmetic.
Power reduction: any power x^k can be expressed as a polynomial of degree less than deg(minpoly) evaluated at x. This is the basis for efficient computation in K[x]/(minpoly).
For idempotent elements (x² = x), the minimal polynomial divides X² - X = X(X-1), so minpoly is either X, X-1, or X(X-1).
Integrality transfers up algebra towers: if x satisfies a monic polynomial over K, mapping it to L[X] gives a monic polynomial over L that still annihilates x.
The key tower theorem: minpoly_L(x) divides map(minpoly_K(x)). This follows because the mapped polynomial annihilates x over L, and the minimal polynomial divides any annihilating polynomial.

Degree consequence: since minpoly_L(x) divides the mapped polynomial (which has the same degree as minpoly_K(x)), we get deg(minpoly_L) ≤ deg(minpoly_K). More polynomials available over L means potentially smaller minimal polynomial.
